title: Best Voice Agent Testing Platforms in 2026: Our Pick and How the Others Compare
summary: The best voice agent testing platforms in 2026: what to look for, why Coval is our pick, and how the other five differ on focus, stage, and price.
body_markdown:
If you’re shortlisting voice agent testing platforms, the demos start to sound alike: simulated callers before launch, scores on your live calls, an alert when quality slips. The differences show up later, when a failed score blocks a release and someone asks whether to believe it, or when your compliance team asks how you know the agent actually did what it told the caller.


> **Quick answer:** Coval is the best voice agent testing platform in 2026. Of the companies built to test AI agents, it’s the most established, and it’s designed for regulated industries. You can measure how far to trust its AI judge, because your own reviewers (or ours) grade a selection of the same calls. And every plan includes the full platform, human review included, from $100 a month with a 7-day free trial. The rest of the field is four early-stage startups (Bluejay, Cekura, Hamming, and Roark) and Cyara, which has tested phone menus for more than 20 years and added AI agent testing in 2026.


We compared the six vendors on five things that decide the purchase, from who built each platform to what it costs to start.


First, a quick snapshot of the six platforms, Coval first and the rest in alphabetical order. Prices come from each vendor’s pricing page and funding from public announcements as of November 2026. The “Built around” column is our summary of each company’s focus.

## What to look for in a voice agent testing platform


Every platform here can run simulated test calls against your agent, and Coval, Bluejay, Cekura, Hamming, and Roark all list SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA, so neither settles the choice. These five things do.


- **Who built it and for whom.** A bank, clinic, or insurer needs a vendor with the track record to pass its security review and a product shaped around regulated work.
- **Whether you can trust the scores.** Behavior scores come from an AI judge, a language model that reads or listens to each call and answers a question you write, such as “Did the agent verify the caller’s identity?” Human review means people on your team label the calls your rules flag, so you can see whether the judge agrees with them.
- **Whether the test callers sound like yours.** Clean, quiet test calls will pass an agent that struggles with accents, background noise, and bad phone lines.
- **How it fits the way you ship.** Tests should run from the terminal, a coding assistant, and CI on every change.
- **What it costs to start.** Check what the entry plan includes and whether you can try it on your own agent first.


The five things that decide the purchase, with Coval's answer to each.


## Coval: the best voice agent testing platform for regulated teams


### Built for regulated industries


Coval is designed for teams that answer to regulators, in[financial services](https://www.coval.ai/industries/financial-services/) ,[healthcare](https://www.coval.ai/industries/healthcare/) , and[insurance](https://www.coval.ai/industries/insurance/) . Chime, a fintech company, tests its voice agents on Coval. On top of the full platform every plan includes, Enterprise adds private or VPC deployment, SAML single sign-on, and custom security reviews.


The track record is there too. We’re a[Y Combinator Summer 2024](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/coval) company and have raised a[$28 million Series A](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-series-a/) , $31 million in total since founding Coval in 2024. Our[founder](https://www.coval.ai/about-us/) , Brooke Hopkins, led the team that built Waymo’s tools for running evaluations of its self-driving cars, and Coval applies the same simulation-first approach to voice agents. And[more than 60 organizations](https://www.coval.ai/blog/new-self-improving-agents/) use Coval, including Zoom, Perplexity, and Fortune 500 enterprises; Zoom’s QA team runs scheduled regression tests on it every day.


### Human review that checks the AI judge


Ask each vendor how you’d know its AI judge is right. Coval’s default judge is a model we fine-tuned ourselves, but we don’t ask you to take its word: the calls your rules flag go to a[review project](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/human-review) , which groups those calls, the metrics to label, and the reviewers assigned to them.


Your rules decide which calls get in. An auto-add rule brings in calls whose metric results match a condition you set, such as calls that failed the AI-disclosure check. Coval decides the order: failures, edge cases, and calls where the judge was least confident go to the front of the queue. Reviewers confirm, override, or annotate each verdict in a[no-code interface](https://www.coval.ai/products/human-review/) , and every change is tracked for audit. Teams without spare reviewers can hand the labeling to ours.


The labels then grade the judge. For each binary (yes-or-no) metric, Coval reports three numbers. Agreement is how often the judge and your reviewers give the same answer. Catch rate is the share of the failures your reviewers found that the judge also flagged. And κ (kappa) is agreement adjusted for the matches you’d get by chance. Agreement alone can flatter a useless metric: in our[docs’ example](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/insights) , reviewers fail 5 of 100 calls, and a judge that passes everything still agrees with them 95% of the time. Its catch rate and its κ are both zero, and those are the numbers that give it away.


Reviews expose the reverse too, a judge failing calls it should pass. One team we[wrote about](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-to-create-ai-judge-metrics-you-can-trust/) tracked whether its outbound agent disclosed that it was an AI, and its metric matched reviewers on 89% of 314 calls. All 35 disagreements were calls where a wrong person picked up or the caller hung up early, before the agent had a chance to disclose anything. As that post puts it, “The agent wasn’t broken. The metric was.”


That settles the first question from the top of this post, whether to believe a failed score. The second, whether the agent actually did what it told the caller, needs no judge at all. If the agent says a card is frozen, is it? After a test call, Coval’s[API State metric](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/deterministic) calls your API, reads the field you name, and compares it with the value you expect, with no model in the loop. Chime uses checks like this to confirm card status, account freezes, and other changes its agent was supposed to make.


### Simulated callers who sound like your callers


A quiet, clear test call is the easiest call your agent will ever get. In Coval, a[persona](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/personas/overview) sets the simulated caller’s voice, language and regional accent, audio environment, and habits, such as how often they interrupt. Noise from Coval’s built-in library, or a recording you upload, plays on the caller’s side for the length of the call, and the line itself can sound like a speakerphone, a landline, a weak cell signal, or a call handing off between cell towers.


How much harder does that make the call? Our public benchmark scores 32 speech-to-text models, the models that turn a caller’s speech into the text an agent acts on, and the figures here are 30-day averages as of November 11, 2026. On clean read speech, the median model gets[4.5%](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-clean) of words wrong. Insert bursts of noise into the same clips and it rises to[6.0%](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-noisegap) , about a third more errors. Re-render them as if spoken far from the microphone and it reaches[6.8%](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-farfield) . Those mistakes happen before your agent decides anything, and a test suite of quiet calls never sees them.


### Runs where your team ships, with the full platform on every plan


The tests that catch regressions are the ones that run on every change, and Coval’s tests run wherever your engineers already make changes. The[Coval CLI](https://docs.coval.ai/welcome) gets you from the terminal to a first simulation in under 15 minutes. AI assistants and coding agents, from Claude to Cursor, can run evaluations through our[MCP connector](https://docs.coval.ai/mcp/overview) and[agent skills](https://docs.coval.ai/agents/skills) . In CI, the[GitHub Action](https://github.com/coval-ai/coval-github-action) fails the build whenever a simulation returns the value you’ve marked as a failure.


On price, every Coval[plan](https://www.coval.ai/pricing/) includes the full platform: simulation, monitoring (scoring your production calls), and human review, with unlimited seats. Starter ($100 a month) and Growth ($500 a month) come with a 7-day free trial. Or skip the setup: give us your agent’s phone number, and our[free audit](https://www.coval.ai/voice-agent-audit/) runs it through 30+ simulations on each behavior you choose, with the report back within two business days.

## How the other voice agent testing platforms compare with Coval


Here are the other five in alphabetical order, not ranked: what each platform is, how you buy it, and where it differs from Coval on the questions above.


### Bluejay


Bluejay, a Y Combinator Spring 2025 company, builds its platform around simulations it generates automatically for voice and chat agents, and you can start free on usage-based pricing. Where it differs, in our view, is focus. Coval is built for regulated teams, whose test results have to satisfy an auditor as well as an engineer.[Coval vs Bluejay](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-vs-bluejay/) goes deeper.


### Cekura


Cekura, a seed-stage company, offers testing and monitoring for voice and chat agents, and in our view it’s weighted toward early-stage teams. Its seat pricing shows the difference: after the first seat, each one costs $30 a month on pay as you go, while every Coval plan has unlimited seats, so adding your fiftieth QA or compliance reviewer costs nothing extra. See[Coval vs Cekura](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-vs-cekura/) for the full comparison.


### Cyara


Cyara has tested scripted phone menus, or IVRs, for more than 20 years, added AI voice agent testing in March 2026, and sells through a demo rather than published prices. Cyara retrofitted a scripted-IVR testing platform to AI agents, while Coval was purpose-built for them.[Coval vs Cyara](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-vs-cyara/) has more.


### Hamming


Hamming, a seed-stage company that quotes its plans after a demo, tests voice and chat agents before launch and monitors their production calls. It serves a broad mix of industries and is less focused on regulated teams than Coval. The two also part ways on the judge: Hamming’s pitch highlights its AI judge’s accuracy, while Coval proves its judge against your own reviewers.[Coval vs Hamming](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-vs-hamming/) has the details.


### Roark


Roark, from Y Combinator’s Winter 2025 batch, tests and monitors voice agents, simulating calls before launch and scoring the calls your agent takes live, on usage-based pricing that scales to Team and Enterprise plans. For a regulated buyer, the gap is track record: Coval has a Series A behind it, and teams like Chime and Zoom already test their agents on it.


## Where built-in platform tests and LLM eval tools fit


If you build on Vapi, Retell, or LiveKit, you already have some testing. Vapi’s[Simulations](https://docs.vapi.ai/test/voice-testing) put an AI tester on the line that “acts as the caller and adapts during a complete conversation.” Retell[runs graded test cases](https://docs.retellai.com/general/introduction) before launch and scores production calls. LiveKit’s[Agent Simulations](https://docs.livekit.io/testing/) run your agent end to end against a simulated user. Inside a single platform, they’re a sensible place to start.


A dedicated platform earns its place when your tests need to outlive any one vendor. Coval is vendor-agnostic by design: it runs the same scenarios across voice AI vendors, so you can compare them with evidence and keep your test suite when you switch. Our[bake-off guide](https://www.coval.ai/blog/voice-ai-platform-comparison-2026-benchmarks-performance-data-and-how-to-choose/) shows how to run that comparison.


LLM evaluation tools such as Langfuse and LangSmith fill a different gap: they trace what your model did at each step and score its text. A voice agent also has to be judged on what the caller heard, which is why Coval’s[audio judges](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/llm-judge) grade the call recording instead of the transcript and its[statistical metrics](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/statistical) measure timing and audio straight from the call. Coval works alongside your tracing rather than replacing it: if you use Langfuse, LangSmith, or Arize Phoenix, Coval[imports those traces](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/simulations/traces/imports) without re-instrumenting your agent.


## How to choose a voice agent testing platform


Whichever platforms make your shortlist, test them on the call your agent most often gets wrong, because that’s the call your compliance team will ask about. On Coval, that test fits inside the 7-day free trial: give the call a noisy persona, put the results in front of your own reviewers in a review project, and point an API State check at the record the call should change. If you’d rather we go first, the free audit runs 30+ simulations against the behaviors you select and returns a scorecard for each.


The trial gives you two answers: whether your reviewers agree with the judge when it fails that call, and whether your records show the agent did what it said. A score you can defend to compliance needs both, and Coval is built to give you both.
